findings.title: AI jargon obscures the actual proposition
findings.evidence: Leverage our multimodal generative narrative engine to synthesise bespoke, heirloom-grade story artefacts from your household's lived-experience corpus.
findings.why: This sounds like technical copy rather than a clear promise to parents, and it tells me nothing concrete about what I receive.

findings.title: Unsubstantiated heirloom claim
findings.evidence: heirloom-grade
findings.why: Durability matters for a physical keepsake, but the page does not explain materials, binding or print quality.

findings.title: Primary creation call to action is vague
findings.evidence: [5] link "Proceed →"
findings.why: Proceed to what? On a marketing page this is slightly lazy, though the surrounding content makes the likely destination inferable.

findings.title: Login fields have no persistent labels
findings.evidence: [5] and [6] are exposed as “textbox (no label)” and only use the placeholders “Email” and “Password”.
findings.why: Placeholder-only naming can become ambiguous for users relying on assistive technology, especially when the fields are filled.

findings.title: Footer links have poor visible contrast
findings.evidence: The screenshot shows “Privacy”, “Terms”, and “Contact” in very pale grey against an off-white background.
findings.why: The legal and contact links are difficult to notice and read, although they do not block the primary login task.

findings.title: Unexplained profile sync error
findings.evidence: “Error 0x80070057: profile sync incomplete.”
findings.why: I cannot tell whether my account state is reliable, and this may affect a book involving Zara’s details or photos.

findings.title: No recovery path for the sync error
findings.evidence: The error banner contains no retry, help, or sign-out control; [6] only offers “+ Create a new book”.
findings.why: I have no way to diagnose or resolve the state before committing personal family information.

findings.title: Personalised greeting uses a generic account label
findings.evidence: “Welcome back, Demo” despite the account email being demo.family@storyhearth.test.
findings.why: It feels like a placeholder account and makes me question whether the right profile loaded.

findings.title: Relationship has an unsafe pre-selection
findings.evidence: [11] combobox "Relationship" (selected: Grandparent)
findings.why: I could accidentally create a story with the wrong family relationship, which is a core part of the book and would be expensive to correct later.

findings.title: Optional second character has a mandatory-looking relationship field
findings.evidence: [10] textbox "Who else is in the story?"; [11] combobox "Relationship" (selected: Grandparent)
findings.why: The interface does not clearly explain whether I should leave the relationship blank when I want Zara to be the only character, making the flow ambiguous.

findings.title: Footer links are very low contrast
findings.evidence: Screenshot: faint footer text for "Privacy", "Terms" and "Contact"
findings.why: I need to inspect privacy terms before uploading or using information about Zara, and the links are difficult to read or locate.

findings.title: Required fields are not identified
findings.evidence: The controls [16], [17], and [18] appear empty, but none is marked required or optional.
findings.why: I cannot tell whether “A special object” is optional, and I may only discover validation rules after pressing Next.

findings.title: Reading levels are expressed only in Lexile jargon
findings.evidence: “Reading level” followed only by “Lexile BR–200L”, “Lexile 200L–500L”, “Lexile 500L–800L”, and “Lexile 800L+”
findings.why: A parent of a seven-year-old does not necessarily know whether a Lexile band is suitable, so the service makes me work out the recommendation myself.

findings.title: Child photo upload lacks accessible visible labelling
findings.evidence: [30] file-upload (no label), immediately below “Upload a clear photo of your child's face...”
findings.why: The surrounding text makes the purpose broadly clear, but a custom upload control without an associated label is worse for screen-reader users and looks unfinished.

findings.title: No immediate privacy explanation for a child's photo
findings.evidence: “Upload a clear photo of your child's face so the illustrations look like them.”
findings.why: A child's biometric appearance is sensitive family data. I need to know whether it is used for model training, who processes it, how long it is retained, and how deletion works before deciding whether to upload.

findings.title: Footer text has extremely low contrast
findings.evidence: The footer labels “Privacy”, “Terms”, “Contact” and copyright appear as very faint beige text on a near-white background.
findings.why: The legal and contact links are hard to see, especially the Privacy link I would normally inspect before uploading family imagery.

findings.title: Loading spinner has no explanatory status
findings.evidence: The central panel contains only an animated circular spinner; the screen provides no visible generation message, expected duration, or submitted-story summary.
findings.why: I cannot tell whether the app is actively generating the book, frozen, or merely navigating, and I cannot verify that the family details were captured correctly.

findings.title: No way to stop or leave generation
findings.evidence: Only global navigation links such as [1]–[5] and footer links [13]–[15] are present; there is no Cancel or Back control in the generation panel.
findings.why: If generation hangs or submits the wrong data, I have no direct way to stop and correct it.

findings.title: Low-contrast footer and weak loading-state affordance
findings.evidence: The footer text, including “Privacy,” “Terms,” and “© 2026 StoryHearth Ltd.”, is extremely faint against the pale background, and the spinner is also low contrast.
findings.why: Faint text is hard to read, particularly for anyone with low vision, and the spinner does not stand out as an active status.

findings.title: Generated title contains a typo
findings.evidence: “The Magical Adventrue of Zara” appears in the heading and cover image
findings.why: A misspelt title makes the finished book feel cheap and undermines confidence in the rest of the generated text.

findings.title: Character description is not reflected in the illustration
findings.evidence: The cover child is labelled Zara but has no visible purple glasses or astronaut hoodie; Dad is not shown.
findings.why: Zara is the hero and the brief specifically included her appearance, so this is a direct failure of personalisation.

findings.title: Cover does not represent the submitted memory
findings.evidence: The cover shows a generic house, Zara, and a purple object, but not the living-room cardboard rocket, Dad, thunderstorm, or moon flag scene.
findings.why: The requested memory is about Zara and Dad building and flying a cardboard rocket; the cover does not establish that story.

findings.title: Page navigation control has weak accessible labelling
findings.evidence: The next control is labelled “›” and the previous control is labelled “‹”
findings.why: The arrow labels are visually compact and do not clearly identify their purpose to assistive technology or keyboard users.

findings.title: Final story sentence is incomplete
findings.evidence: “And from that day on, whenever Zara looked up at the sky, she would always remember”
findings.why: A truncated sentence is an obvious generation failure in a paid keepsake, and it makes the book feel unready to print.

findings.title: Generated characters and story props lose supplied details
findings.evidence: The page labels only “Zara,” while the illustration shows no purple glasses or astronaut hoodie, Dad, cardboard rocket, or purple-sock flag.
findings.why: The book is meant to personalise our actual family memory, but these generic images are not faithful to the character descriptions and story brief.

findings.title: Premium gift wrap is pre-selected
findings.evidence: [6] checkbox "Premium gift wrap" (checked); it adds "£7.99"
findings.why: I do not want an unsolicited £7.99 add-on, and pre-ticked extras make the total harder to trust.

findings.title: No preview approval or return policy is visible before payment
findings.evidence: The only order action shown is [11] "Pay now"; the page shows the title and price but no preview link, edit control, or cancellation policy.
findings.why: I need to know that I can inspect or correct the generated book before committing £45.97, especially after the preview was visibly wrong.

findings.title: Delivery estimate and address requirements are missing
findings.evidence: The page shows “Shipping & handling £12.99” and a single textbox [7] “Address”, with no delivery date or address guidance.
findings.why: I cannot assess the value or delivery risk of a £45.97 purchase without an expected date or clear address requirements.

findings.title: Misspelled generated title is carried into checkout
findings.evidence: [5] "Hardcover: The Magical Adventrue of Zara"
findings.why: The misspelling confirms the faulty generated output is being used as the order title, and I would not want to pay for it.

findings.title: Pre-ticked gift wrap raises the total
findings.evidence: [6] checkbox "Premium gift wrap" (checked) and "Total £45.97"
findings.why: This is an unsolicited £7.99 charge that makes the displayed total misleadingly higher than the base order.

findings.title: No order cancellation or correction path is visible
findings.evidence: No cancel, edit, review, or return control is visible around the [11] "Pay now" action.
findings.why: I need control before paying, not a one-way checkout based on a flawed generated preview.

findings.title: fidelity
findings.evidence: The title reads “The Magical Adventrue of Zara,” but the supplied story involved Zara and Dad building a cardboard rocket, flying to the Moon, and planting a purple-sock flag.

findings.title: character_consistency
findings.evidence: Zara is depicted as bald and wearing a plain teal shirt, not with “Black hair in two puffs, purple glasses, astronaut hoodie.”

findings.title: text_image_fit
findings.evidence: The cover supplies only a house, Zara, sun, and detached sock; it does not visually establish the stated “Magical Adventure.”

findings.title: language
findings.evidence: “Adventrue” is misspelled; the correct word is “Adventure.”

findings.title: visual_quality
findings.evidence: The image is clean but extremely sparse, with the purple sock floating in midair and no convincing connection to the story.

findings.title: emotional_resonance
findings.evidence: The generic house scene omits Dad, the handmade rocket, the storm, and the shared imaginative adventure that made the memory personal.

findings.title: language
findings.evidence: The page visibly contains “{{recipient_name}}” and “{{sender_name}}” as raw template placeholders.

findings.title: fidelity
findings.evidence: The child and sender were known to be Zara and Dad, yet neither is inserted into the dedication.

findings.title: visual_quality
findings.evidence: The large book panel is almost empty, and unresolved template syntax appears in the middle of the page.

findings.title: emotional_resonance
findings.evidence: A personalized dedication should make the book feel like a keepsake, but the placeholder text makes it feel broken and automated.

findings.title: fidelity
findings.evidence: The text says “in Our living room,” but the picture shows Zara outdoors beside a house and the purple sock floats separately.

findings.title: fidelity
findings.evidence: Dad and the cardboard rocket are absent even though both are central to the supplied memory.

findings.title: character_consistency
findings.evidence: Zara again has no black hair in two puffs, purple glasses, or astronaut hoodie.

findings.title: language
findings.evidence: “in Our living room” has unnecessary capitalization, and “loved nothing more than A purple sock used as a flag” treats a form label as a noun phrase.

findings.title: age_fit
findings.evidence: The opening uses the awkward construction “loved nothing more than A purple sock used as a flag,” which is not natural early-reader language.

findings.title: text_image_fit
findings.evidence: The text explicitly locates the scene in the living room, while the image depicts an exterior lawn and detached house.

findings.title: age_fit
findings.evidence: The sentence uses “ephemeral,” “luminescence,” “crepuscular,” “engendered,” “melancholy,” “juxtaposing,” “ineffable,” and “existential trepidation.” The measured grade level is 7.6 for a requested reading age of 7.

findings.title: fidelity
findings.evidence: The text invents unexplained sadness and existential fear, while the supplied memory centered on a shared, exciting pretend space journey.

findings.title: character_consistency
findings.evidence: Zara remains bald and wears a teal shirt instead of her specified black puff hairstyle, purple glasses, and astronaut hoodie.

findings.title: text_image_fit
findings.evidence: The picture supports the simple idea of looking at the sky, but Zara appears to stare forward rather than clearly upward, and the scene still shows the exterior house rather than the living room.

findings.title: text_image_fit
findings.evidence: The text says “the rain began to pour” and describes raindrops and puddles, but I5 shows a bright sun and no rain or puddles.

findings.title: language
findings.evidence: Zara's name is misspelled as “Zar,” and the phrase “holding A purple sock used as a flag tight” has incorrect ordering and capitalization.

findings.title: fidelity
findings.evidence: Zara is supposed to be wearing an astronaut hoodie, but the text merely says she “pulled up her hood”; the image shows no hoodie at all.

findings.title: character_consistency
findings.evidence: Zara is still bald and wears a teal shirt, with no purple glasses or recognizable purple-puff hairstyle.

findings.title: age_fit
findings.evidence: “Then the rain began to pour” and “holding … tight” produce awkward rhythms rather than natural language for an emerging reader.

findings.title: fidelity
findings.evidence: The page invents “Uncle Bartholomew,” an important character absent from every supplied story field.

findings.title: fidelity
findings.evidence: The requested co-character, “Dad (Daniel),” is replaced by Uncle Bartholomew and the cardboard-rocket launch is omitted.

findings.title: coherence
findings.evidence: “Zara, follow me!” he called, and he followed him along the winding path” switches from Zara to an unidentified male pronoun and then to another male pronoun.

findings.title: age_fit
findings.evidence: The sudden appearance of a shadowy stranger and instruction to follow him is more ominous than the supplied playful father-daughter memory.

findings.title: text_image_fit
findings.evidence: The image supports the two figures and a lantern but does not show the stated winding path; Zara's astronaut hoodie, glasses, hair, sock flag, Dad, and rocket are all missing.

findings.title: visual_quality
findings.evidence: The printed labels “Uncle Bartholomew” and “Zara” sit awkwardly across the lower part of the illustration like debugging text.

findings.title: fidelity
findings.evidence: The page invents a dark forest, threatening shadows, and “a shiny red balloon,” none of which appeared in the supplied story.

findings.title: fidelity
findings.evidence: The cardboard rocket, Dad, living room, and purple-sock flag are absent at the point where the lunar journey should be developing.

findings.title: age_fit
findings.evidence: “the shadows grew teeth and whispered that no one would ever find Zara again” introduces explicit loss-of-safety horror and may be too frightening for a seven-year-old.

findings.title: text_image_fit
findings.evidence: The text says the shadows grew teeth, but the visible shadows are plain green trees without teeth; the red balloon is visible, but its significance is unexplained.

findings.title: character_consistency
findings.evidence: Zara is still bald and dressed in the same teal shirt rather than wearing her supplied purple glasses and astronaut hoodie.

findings.title: coherence
findings.evidence: “Once upon a time, in Our living room, there lived a curious child named Zara” repeats the opening almost verbatim instead of advancing the plot.

findings.title: fidelity
findings.evidence: The supplied climax—flying to the Moon and planting Zara's purple-sock flag—never occurs. Dad and the cardboard rocket are absent.

findings.title: language
findings.evidence: “skipped all way home” is ungrammatical; it should be “skipped all the way home.”

findings.title: text_image_fit
findings.evidence: The text says Zara skipped home, but she is standing motionless beside the house. The image provides no visual indication of returning or of the completed Moon adventure.

findings.title: character_consistency
findings.evidence: Zara again has the same bald, teal-shirt appearance, not her black puffs, purple glasses, and astronaut hoodie.

findings.title: coherence
findings.evidence: “whenever Zara looked up at the sky, she would always remember” ends without identifying what she remembered.

findings.title: language
findings.evidence: “The End” appears twice, and the final sentence has no completion or final punctuation.

findings.title: fidelity
findings.evidence: The closing image omits Dad, the cardboard rocket, the Moon, and the purple-sock flag that constitute the supplied memory.

findings.title: text_image_fit
findings.evidence: The image contains “The End,” but it does not visually support the unfinished reflection about Zara remembering the shared experience.

findings.title: emotional_resonance
findings.evidence: The final page ends abruptly and omits the father-daughter moment, so it does not feel personal or keepsake-worthy.

findings.title: character_consistency
findings.evidence: Zara remains bald and wears a teal shirt instead of the specified hairstyle, glasses, and astronaut hoodie.
